html:
The Guarani are an Indigenous people of the forests and river valleys of southern South America, in what is now Paraguay, southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina and eastern Bolivia. Tekohá is their word for a home territory: the place where a community can live in its own way.

They speak Guarani, one of the Tupi-Guarani languages, and are close kin of the coastal Tupi. Around 1492 they lived in villages of large houses, cleared forest to grow maize and manioc, and moved their fields and villages every few years.

The Spanish founded Asunción in 1537 with Guarani help, and many Spanish men married Guarani women. From 1609 the Jesuit reductions gathered tens of thousands of Guarani into mission towns until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767. Portuguese slave raiders from São Paulo attacked those missions repeatedly.

Today the main Guarani groups are the Mbya, the Ava Guarani or Ñandeva and the Pai Tavyterã or Kaiowá. Guarani is an official language of Paraguay and is spoken by most Paraguayans.
